newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia, China, C. Asian states to sign border pact.
newsitem.headline: Russia, China, C. Asian states to sign border pact.

text.p: The leaders of Russia, China, Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan and Kazakhstan sign a treaty on Thursday intended to remove the risk of confrontation along the vast former Soviet-Chinese border.

The signing ceremony in Moscow follows talks on Wednesday between Russian President Boris Yeltsin and Chinese President Jiang Zemin which were crowned by a declaration outlining their vision of a post-Cold War world with no dominant superpower.

"The border treaty will finally end confrontation between Beijing and former Soviet republics," Interfax news agency quoted Kazakhstan's borderguards chief, Major General Toktasyn Buzubayev, as saying.
Border clashes in 1969 marked the climax of hostility between the Soviet Union and China, whose alliance of the 1950s collapsed into rivalry for leadership of the communist world.

Relations between Beijing and Moscow have been gradually improving since 1989 and the independent states left by the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 have been establishing friendly relations with China.

Few details of the border treaty have been made public. Kazakh President Nursultan Nazarbayev's spokesman said the five states would reduce forces deployed near the border and pull them back about 100 km (60 miles).
But Interfax quoted a Russian foreign ministry official as saying the treaty did not envisage pulling back troops.
"The agreement does not provide for any troop withdrawal but rather concerns control of their numbers," the official said.
Russia has snuggled up to China since its honeymoon with the West ended over NATO's decision to offer membership to some eastern European countries. Moscow sees that as a threat to its security.
Russia is jealous of the United States' leading world role and China resents Western criticism over human rights.
But both countries have made clear they will not be driven back into the closeness of the 1950s and want instead to forge a "strategic partnership".
The declaration signed on Wednesday by Jiang and Yeltsin outlined some of the partnership's aims.
"No country should seek hegemony, practice power politics or monopolise international affairs," it said, without mentioning any specific country but clearly with the United States in mind.
The declaration implicitly referred to NATO enlargement.

"Both sides express concern over attempts to enlarge and strengthen military blocs because such a tendency may pose a threat to the security of some countries and aggravate regional and global tensions," it said.
Yeltsin's press secretary, Sergei Yastrzhembsky, made clear Moscow viewed the declaration as a major foreign policy victory. "One may talk about a breakthrough in Russian policy in Asia," he said.
Chinese spokesman Shen Guofang said Jiang had invited Yeltsin to visit China whenever was convenient for the Kremlin leader, and that he was likely to go next November.

"President Yeltsin jokingly told Chairman Jiang that his readiness (to come) is so obvious that the two leaders do not need to involve diplomatic services to arrange the visit," he said, reflecting the improved relations.
Yeltsin and Jiang hold more talks on Thursday, when the Chinese leader will also meet Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.
